articles.title: Modern Warfare 4 Adds Tactical Sprint to Blood Rush
articles.excerpt: Modern Warfare 4 removes Tactical Sprint by default in the Beta, moves it to Blood Rush, and slows slides to create more grounded combat.
articles.content:
The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Beta movement update removes Tactical Sprint as a default ability and moves it to the Blood Rush Perk, while reducing slide effectiveness and making several mobility adjustments.

Infinity Ward detailed the latest Beta patch on August 28. In addition to the movement changes, they updated the time-to-kill (TTK) again. After the previous TTK update, they still wanted to increase it, albeit slightly. So they updated the weapons to increase survivability and create more room for skill expression.

  • RELATED: Modern Warfare 4 Beta PC Specs & Requirements Revealed

Modern Warfare 4 Adds Tactical Sprint to Blood Rush

To address players’ movement issues, the developers removed Tactical Sprint by default; it’s now a perk and has been enhanced by reducing its sprint-to-fire speed penalty. Infinity Ward adds that this is only a beta experiment and reminds players that their voice matters.

If they stick with the change, they will also need to consider its place alongside other perks. You can see the full breakdown of movement changes below.

MOVEMENT

We saw a lot of feedback about Tactical Sprint over Weekend 1, and we know there are a range of opinions about it. We have removed Tactical Sprint by default, which we think improves the pace of combat and gives the game a more classic feel. For players who prefer a faster playstyle, we moved it to a Perk and enhanced it by reducing its sprint-to-fire speed penalty. We have also adjusted Tac Sprint and slide speeds to rebalance them against each other.

This is an experiment for Beta which we hope improves the pace of the game and enhances player choice. If we decide to stick with this change, we need to consider its place in the Perk table and which other adjustments to Perks go along with it.

  • Tac Sprint
    • Moved Tactical Sprint to the Blood Rush Perk.
    • Reduced Tactical Sprint sprint-to-fire time to match base sprint.
    • Reduced Tactical Sprint speed by 4%.
  • Sprint Speeds
    • Increased knife base sprint speeds.
    • Increased all pistol base sprint speeds.
  • Slide Adjustments
    • Increased slide-to-jump delay.
    • Reduced slide distance by 10%.
    • Reduced slide speed by 9%.
  • Stamina
    • Reduced stamina by 8%.
  • Mantle
    • Fixed an issue where players could mantle much higher than intended.
  • Climbing
    • Fixed an issue that caused stutters when climbing ladders and pipes.

articles.title: 2029 Lotus Esprit to Offer V-6 Option Alongside Hybrid V-8, CEO Confirms
articles.excerpt: We already knew about the nearly 1000-hp hybrid V-8 Lotus is planning, but a new report suggests it’ll be paired with a V-6 option.
articles.content:
We already knew about the nearly 1000-hp hybrid V-8 Lotus is planning, but a new report suggests it’ll be paired with a V-6 option.

  • Lotus is planning to give the upcoming Esprit supercar (codenamed Type 135) a V-6 option, the automaker’s CEO said during a call, Autocar reported.
  • The V-6 option will join the planned hybrid V-8, which is expected to produce roughly 1000 horsepower and serve to fulfil the brand’s commitment to lightness.
  • The reveal and launch of the revived Esprit are both planned for 2028, with more details of the model expected soon.

Few founders have left such a strong mark on their company that their ethos remains the driving force of the company even decades after their death, but if such a list exists, Colin Chapman can certainly be counted among its ranks. In the spirit of building lightweight cars—something Chapman famously approved of—Lotus will add a V-6 option to its upcoming Esprit, internally known as Type 135, the brand’s CEO said during a recent earnings call, Autocar reported.

The hybrid V-6 option will allow Lotus to comply with tightening global emissions regulations, “while preserving essential Lotus DNA of lightweight engineering and extreme track-focused driving dynamics,” Feng Qingfeng, the brand’s CEO, said during a recent investor relations call. It will join the previously confirmed V-8 hybrid that Lotus is planning for the new flagship model.

While not confirmed by Lotus, the Esprit’s V-6 will almost certainly be the same hybrid V-6 the brand has planned for the updated Emira. In that car, the powertrain consists of a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6, paired with an automatic transmission and an integrated electric motor. In the Emira’s case, the powertrain is reportedly good for up to 536 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque, though we wouldn’t be shocked to see larger figures for the Esprit.

Like the hybrid V-8, the new V-6 is being produced by Horse, the joint venture company owned by Renault and Lotus's parent company, Geely. The larger engine is poised to produce a combined output of at least 986 horsepower and will pair with an eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox. And, despite its higher cylinder count, Lotus is putting considerable effort into keeping the powertrain’s weight down.

The Type 135 was originally planned as an electric successor to the Emira before changing market conditions forced Lotus to alter its plans. The full reveal and start of production for the revived Esprit are both planned for 2028. We expect more information about the model to be drip-fed in the coming months until the car’s eventual arrival.

“The Type 135 will fill the gap between the Emira and Evija, preserving the emotional connection Emira owners have with the Lotus mechanical handling, while leveraging V-8 hybrid technology to approach the technical benchmark set by the Evija,” Qingfeng reportedly told Autocar.

articles.title: Can PLTR Stock Live Up To Its Multiple?
articles.excerpt: This is a hyper-growth chapter for Palantir Technologies. The company now provides a complete sovereign AI stack, with its AIP platform as the core engine for government and commercial clients. This explosive U.S. growth
articles.content:
This is a hyper-growth chapter for Palantir Technologies. The company now provides a complete sovereign AI stack, with its AIP platform as the core engine for government and commercial clients.

This explosive U.S. growth is creating immense demand that strains the company’s ability to scale. In response, management is now actively searching for technically competent partners to help meet this demand.

That’s the story the market is currently paying 147.9x trailing earnings for. Has it taken the multiple too far, or is the growth implied by today’s price reasonable? Let’s unpack below.

Before we get into the math behind that valuation, PLTR‘s current numbers are worth keeping in mind as a reference point:

LTM refers to last twelve months.

What The Price Is Asking For

To defend PLTR’s $446.2B market cap over the next 7 years, three things have to play out. The multiple settles from today’s 147.9x toward 28.8x, the multiple a mature, scaled software franchise typically settles into. Margins land near 35%, set near the midpoint of the company’s own margin cycle, since its peak clears mature peers but its through-cycle average sits well below that peak. And revenue compounds from $6.2B today to $44.3B at maturity, supporting $15.5B of annual net income. That last line works out to a required revenue CAGR of 33%, below the 79% the business is currently running.

Is This Realistic?

Growth is being driven by accelerating adoption in the U.S. commercial segment. Existing customers are also expanding their use from the Foundry platform to the full Ontology and AI stack. The company is also entering the market for fine-tuning models, expanding its role beyond orchestration.

The company’s current growth and margins are at a cyclical peak, far above its historical average. Management has already signaled a significant expense ramp for the coming quarter due to new hiring. This spending, combined with a heavy reliance on the booming U.S. market, creates risk of margin reversion if growth moderates.

Today’s price needs less growth than the business is currently delivering. But that current pace is a cyclical peak, not a sustainable rate. In a normal year, the bar is meaningfully higher.

The challenge is finding enough competent partners to scale its U.S. boom before cyclical pressures cause margins to revert.

For a different read on PLTR, see our recent piece Palantir Technologies Stock Surged On Evidence That Was Already Public.

Should You Invest In Palantir Technologies?

Reverse-engineering the growth baked into today’s high multiples reveals a thin margin for error. A single-stock thesis at these valuations is inherently fragile. As historical volatility shows, relying on the priced-for-perfection math of one position ignores the structural risk that high-multiple names face during broader market inflections. The solution is a rule-based portfolio approach.

If it is exposure to software as a whole you want rather than this one name, a software ETF like IGV covers that single sector. Going broader than any one sector, to a quality-first mix across the whole market, is where the portfolio below comes in.
